headline: Omatsuri is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 祭り (matsuri, “festival”).

sources.quote: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 祭り (matsuri, “festival”).

headline: Mezurashii ultimately comes from the verb 愛づ (medu), whose descendant 愛でる (mederu) means “to love; to admire”.

sources.quote: From classical -na adjective 珍(めずら) (mezura) + しい (-shii, adjective-forming suffix).
Ultimately from Old Japanese verb 愛づ (medu, medzu), modern Japanese 愛でる (mederu, “to love; to admire, to appreciate”).

The meaning originally referred to something that was admirable or favorable, something that had value, as an extension of the underlying verb. This meaning is used in the Man'yōshū, dating to the mid-700s. This further extended to indicate something that was rare or unusual in ways that one would find notable or attractive, and this meaning was also already used in the Man'yōshū. Over time, the admirable sense weakened, and the rare sense became dominant.
Cognate with Northern Amami Ōshima 珍っさり (むぃずぃらっさり, mïzïrassari).

meaning: to take (something) out; to hand in (something)
headline: Dasu is the causative form of 出づ (idu): いだす (idasu) in Old Japanese.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese いだす (idasu), the causative form of 出づ (idu) Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *intasu.
First cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.

headline: Daigaku is from Middle Chinese 大學 (MC dajH haewk).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 大學 (MC dajH haewk).

headline: Kuraberu is the modern lower monograde descendant of an old lower bigrade verb, 比ぶ.

sources.quote: Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 比ぶ entry.

headline: Hima is probably 間 (hi, “free time”) plus 間 (ma, “space, interval”), and the first may relate to 皹 (hibi, “chap of the skin”).

sources.quote: Probably a compound of 間 (hi, “free time”, possibly related to 皹 (hibi, “chap of the skin”)) + 間 (ma, “space, interval”).

meaning: two days before yesterday, three days ago
headline: Sakiototoi is 先 (saki, “previous”) plus 一昨日 (ototoi, “day before yesterday”); the kanji spelling is jukujikun.

sources.quote: Compound of 先(さき) (saki, “previous”) + 一昨日(おととい) (ototoi, “day before yesterday”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

headline: Koshi first appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kəsi.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE. In turn from Proto-Japonic *kəsi.

headline: Mata is from Proto-Japonic *mata, cognate with Miyako and Okinawan mata.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mata. Cognate with Miyako 股 (また, mata), Okinawan 股 (また, mata).

headline: Tsutome is the continuative stem of 勤める (tsutomeru).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 勤(つと)める (tsutomeru).

headline: Maru shifted from Old Japanese 丸 (maro), and is related to 麻呂 (maro).

sources.quote: ⟨maro₂⟩ → */marə/ → /maru/
Shift from Old Japanese 丸 (maro, see below).
Related to 麻(ま)呂(ろ) (maro).

headline: Higeki is a calque of English tragedy, built from 悲 (hi, “sad, sorrowful”) plus 劇 (geki, “drama; play”).

sources.quote: Calque of English tragedy, from Middle Chinese-derived elements 悲(ひ) (hi, “sad, sorrowful”) + 劇(げき) (geki, “drama; play”).

headline: Sumai is the continuative stem of 住まう (sumau, “to live at; to dwell; to reside”), first attested in the 970s.

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 住(す)まう (sumau, “to live at; to dwell; to reside”).
First attested in the 970s.

meaning: to store to pay, to supply
headline: Osameru is cognate with 治める (osameru) and 修める (osameru).

sources.quote: Cognate with Japanese 治(おさ)める (osameru) and 修(おさ)める (osameru).

meaning: to exchange, to interchange, to substitute
headline: This kaeru, written 換, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the lower bigrade pattern.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 変(か)える (kaeru), 替(か)える (kaeru) and 代(か)える (kaeru).

sources.quote: Compound of 丸 (maru, “round; (by extension) entirety”) + ごと (-goto).

headline: Tobikomu is tobi, the stem of 飛ぶ (tobu, “to jump; to fly”), plus 込む (komu, “to go into”).

sources.quote: Compound of 飛(と)び (tobi, “jumping”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 飛(と)ぶ (tobu, “to jump; to fly”)) + 込(こ)む (komu, “to go into”).

sources.quote: Compound of 長 (“long; elder”) + 女 (“woman; female”).

sources.quote: First attested in Shinsarugakuki (11th century) as 將基, but also later as 象戯 or 象棋 in other literatures. Probably cognate with Chinese 象棋 (xiàngqí).

headline: Dōmo is どう (dō, “how”) plus も (mo, “ever, even, also”): close in meaning to “no matter how”.

sources.quote: Derived as compound of どう (dō, “how”, question word) + も (mo, “ever, even, also”, particle). Literal meaning is close to “no matter how, howsoever, in all cases”. Idiomatically and semantically used as an intensifier in specific contexts. Compare とても (totemo, “very”).

sources.quote: Reduplication of 色(いろ) (iro, “colour; type; kind”).

headline: Shimekiri is the stem of 締め切る (shimekiru): 締め (shime, “fastening, locking, shutting”) plus 切り (kiri).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 締(し)め切(き)る (shimekiru). By surface analysis, 締(し)め (shime, “fastening, locking, shutting”) + 切(き)り (kiri).
